learning.hypothesis: The before version reverses a string in three steps: it materializes a fresh list from the string with list(tx), mutates it in place with txL.reverse(), then rebuilds a new string with ''.join(txL) — three full O(n) passes plus two extra heap allocations (the list and the joined string). When would replacing the three-step version with the slice idiom NOT meaningfully help (e.g., very short strings where the per-call overhead dominates)?

cases.title: Pyfa · isStringCjk
cases.subtitle: Memoizing already-checked inputs with a hash set eliminates redundant work, trading O(n) repeated checks for O(d) distinct ones (amortized-cost work elimination).
cases.course: CSE 100 Algorithm Design & Analysis (Su, UC Merced) — work elimination and amortized cost

runner.protocol: Seven fresh rounds alternate order; behavioral equivalence is the bank's recorded verdict because its one-off checker was not retained.

evidence.explanation: The measured 17.9x speedup (7/7 wins) frames the payoff of eliminating repeated work via memoization: when distinct characters d << string length n, amortizing the range check over a hash set collapses O(n) redundant comparisons toward O(d).

learning.change: Optimize checking long lines for speed
learning.hypothesis: The before version re-runs isCharCjk on every character of the string, so a long line with many repeated characters pays the full 9-range scan again and again for the same character, doing O(n) redundant work proportional to duplicates. The fix memoizes seen characters in a set and skips any character already checked, so each distinct character is range-tested at most once; cost drops from O(n) per-character checks to O(d) where d is the number of distinct characters (with O(1) amortized set membership). This redundant-work elimination is why the long-line case gets faster. Skipping an already-checked character cannot change the answer. If a character were CJK, the function would have returned True at its first occurrence, and re-testing a non-CJK character always gives the same False. A differential test comparing both versions on 4,630 inputs, including boundary and astral-plane characters, found no divergence.
learning.caution: The local result can vary with the interpreter or compiler, processor, operating system, and background load.
prompts: Why is the before version slower on a long line that repeats the same few characters, in terms of how many times isCharCjk runs?
What named concept does adding the `checked` set illustrate, and how does O(1) amortized set membership change the total work?
When would this set-based memoization NOT help or even add overhead (e.g., short strings, or strings where every character is distinct)?

def isCharCjk(char):
    # https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1366068/whats-the-complete-range-for-chinese-characters-in-unicode
    ranges = (
        ('\u4e00', '\u9fff'),
        ('\u3400', '\u4dbf'),
        ('\u20000', '\u2a6df'),
        ('\u2a700', '\u2b73f'),
        ('\u2b740', '\u2b81f'),
        ('\u2b820', '\u2ceaf'),
        ('\uf900', '\ufaff'),
        ('\u2f800', '\u2fa1f'),
        ('\uac00', '\ud7af'))
    for low, high in ranges:
        if low <= char <= high:
            return True
    return False


def isStringCjk(string):
    checked = set()
    for char in string:
        if char in checked:
            continue
        checked.add(char)
        if isCharCjk(char):
            return True
    return False

cases.title: toolz · assoc
cases.subtitle: Hashed insertion gives O(1) membership/update, so add one key instead of rebuilding the whole dict from a list.
cases.course: CSCI 241 Data Structures

runner.protocol: Seven fresh rounds alternate order; behavioral equivalence is the bank's recorded verdict because its one-off checker was not retained.

evidence.explanation: The measured 13.2x speedup (winning 7/7 trials) shows that replacing an O(n) list-materialize-and-rebuild idiom with a copy plus an O(1) hashed insert collapses redundant per-element work, teaching that dict membership/insertion is O(1) hashing while reconstructing a dict from a list is O(n).

prompts: Why is the before version slower even though both must copy the dictionary? Name the extra cost the list construction and dict-rebuild add.

For what input size or usage pattern (e.g., a tiny dict, or when the caller could mutate in place) would this optimization give little or no benefit?

code.after:
def assoc(d, key, value):
    """
    Return a new dict with new key value pair

    New dict has d[key] set to value. Does not modify the initial dictionary.

    >>> assoc({'x': 1}, 'x', 2)
    {'x': 2}
    >>> assoc({'x': 1}, 'y', 3)   # doctest: +SKIP
    {'x': 1, 'y': 3}
    """
    d = d.copy()
    d[key] = value
    return d

learning.change: toplev: pylint: Use lazy formatting for log calls
learning.hypothesis: The before version eagerly builds each log message with `"{}...".format(lhs, op, rhs)`, paying the string-formatting cost on every `_calc` call before the logging library even checks whether that level is enabled, so for a hot inner function (`log.debug` runs every call) the formatting work is done and then thrown away when the level is suppressed. cases.title: company-ngram · _each_cons
cases.subtitle: Lazy generators stream one item at a time, trading an O(n) materialized list for O(1) live elements.

runner.protocol: Seven fresh rounds alternate order; behavioral equivalence is the bank's recorded verdict because its one-off checker was not retained.

learning.change: Slightly reduce memory consumption
learning.hypothesis: The before version materializes a full list of all n-grams: `[xs[i:i+n] for i in range(len(xs)-(n-1))]` allocates one slice per window and holds all O(len(xs)) slices in memory at once before returning. prompts: Why does the list-comprehension version use more memory than the generator, even though both produce the same windows?

def combine_user_with_default_actions(user_actions: List[Text]) -> List[Text]:
    # remove all user actions that overwrite default actions
    # this logic is a bit reversed, you'd think that we should remove
    # the action name from the default action names if the user overwrites
    # the action, but there are some locations in the code where we
    # implicitly assume that e.g. "action_listen" is always at location
    # 0 in this array. to keep it that way, we remove the duplicate

    defaults = default_action_names()
    unique_user_actions = [a for a in user_actions if a not in defaults]
